stem:
A 39-year-old man newly diagnosed with HIV attends your general practice for review of his baseline results. He is asymptomatic apart from mild oral candidiasis. He is starting to consider antiretroviral therapy and is anxious about opportunistic infections. He has no other medical conditions and takes no regular medications.

On examination he is well nourished. Oral thrush is confirmed on the palate. Chest is clear and there is no lymphadenopathy. Baseline results show CD4 count 180 cells/microL (500-1500), HIV viral load 92000 copies/mL, hepatitis B surface antigen negative, hepatitis C antibody negative, syphilis serology negative, Toxoplasma IgG positive, and QuantiFERON-TB Gold negative. Renal function and liver enzymes are within normal limits. He is fully immunised for age. His G6PD status is normal on screening.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76/min, blood pressure 122/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Well nourished, oral candida on palate, no lymphadenopathy, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: CD4 180 cells/mcL (500-1500); HIV RNA 92000 copies/mL; Toxoplasma IgG positive; QuantiFERON-TB Gold negative; UEC and LFTs within normal limits; G6PD normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate opportunistic infection prophylaxis to commence today?

options.text: Oral azithromycin 1200 mg once weekly as Mycobacterium avium complex prophylaxis for the current CD4 count
options.rationale: MAC prophylaxis is no longer routinely recommended by ASHM when antiretroviral therapy is being initiated, regardless of CD4; PCP prophylaxis is the immediate need. (Source: ASHM Australian Commentary on HIV Guidelines)
source_refs: ASHM Australian Commentary on HIV Guidelines

options.text: Oral fluconazole 200 mg daily as primary prophylaxis against cryptococcal meningitis and oesophageal candidiasis
options.rationale: Primary cryptococcal prophylaxis is not standard AU practice at CD4 above 100; treat oral thrush with topical or short-course fluconazole and start PCP prophylaxis. (Source: ASHM Australian Commentary on HIV Guidelines)
source_refs: ASHM Australian Commentary on HIV Guidelines

options.text: Oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 160/800 mg one tablet daily as Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia prophylaxis
options.rationale: CD4 below 200 cells/microL is the ASHM threshold for primary Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia prophylaxis with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole; his Toxoplasma-positive status also gets covered by this regimen. (Source: ASHM Australian Commentary on HIV Guidelines)
source_refs: ASHM Australian Commentary on HIV Guidelines

options.text: Oral isoniazid 300 mg daily plus pyridoxine 25 mg for 9 months of latent tuberculosis treatment as the priority prophylaxis
options.rationale: His QuantiFERON is negative; latent TB treatment is not indicated, and PCP prophylaxis is the immediate need. (Source: ASHM Australian Commentary on HIV Guidelines)
source_refs: ASHM Australian Commentary on HIV Guidelines

options.text: Oral valaciclovir 500 mg twice daily as chronic herpes simplex virus suppression indefinitely while CD4 remains low
options.rationale: HSV suppression is only indicated when there are frequent recurrences, not as a routine primary prophylaxis at CD4 180 without HSV history. (Source: ASHM Australian Commentary on HIV Guidelines)
source_refs: ASHM Australian Commentary on HIV Guidelines

explanation.summary: Opportunistic infection prophylaxis in HIV is CD4-count driven. Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia prophylaxis with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 160/800 mg daily (or 3 times weekly) starts at CD4 below 200 cells/microL, or with a history of AIDS-defining illness, and continues until CD4 is above 200 for at least 3 months on suppressive ART. This regimen also covers Toxoplasma reactivation, which is the concern above CD4 100 in Toxoplasma-IgG-positive patients. Mycobacterium avium complex prophylaxis is no longer routinely recommended if effective ART is being started. Primary cryptococcal, fungal or herpes virus prophylaxis is not routine. Latent TB treatment follows a positive QuantiFERON-TB Gold or Mantoux; a positive screen prompts a 4-month rifampicin or 9-month isoniazid course.
key_points: PCP prophylaxis with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole at CD4 below 200.
Same regimen covers Toxoplasma reactivation in IgG-positive patients.
MAC prophylaxis no longer routine on modern ART.
Latent TB treatment only for QuantiFERON-positive patients.
explanation.pearls: Any patient with HIV and CD4 below 200 cells/microL starts trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 160/800 mg daily for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and Toxoplasma cover.

sources.label: ASHM Australian Commentary on HIV Guidelines
Australian eTG: Antibiotic - HIV opportunistic infections

stem:
A 32-year-old nurse returns to your general practice after employer screening. She emigrated from the Philippines 4 years ago, has no known TB contact and is a healthy non-smoker on no regular medications. She has never had a chest infection and denies fever, night sweats, weight loss or productive cough. She feels well.

On examination her chest is clear, there is no cervical lymphadenopathy and vital signs are normal. Her QuantiFERON-TB Gold test is positive (interferon-gamma 1.8 IU/mL). Chest radiograph shows no infiltrate, cavitation or lymphadenopathy. HIV serology is negative. Liver enzymes are within normal limits. She wants to know whether she has tuberculosis and what should happen next.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 68/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Well, no lymphadenopathy, chest clear, no scars
data_table.Investigations: QuantiFERON-TB Gold positive (IFN-gamma 1.8 IU/mL); CXR: no infiltrate or cavitation; HIV serology negative; LFTs within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Reassure that this is a false-positive result from BCG vaccination in childhood and no further follow-up is required
options.rationale: QuantiFERON-TB Gold does not cross-react with BCG; a positive result indicates Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection, either latent or active. (Source: NTAC Position Statement on Latent TB Infection)
source_refs: NTAC Position Statement on Latent TB Infection

options.text: Commence rifampicin-isoniazid-pyrazinamide-ethambutol quadruple therapy empirically today as directly observed therapy
options.rationale: Quadruple therapy is treatment for active TB; her chest radiograph and symptom review are negative so this is latent TB, which requires a single-agent regimen. (Source: NTAC Position Statement on Latent TB Infection)
source_refs: NTAC Position Statement on Latent TB Infection

options.text: Repeat the QuantiFERON-TB Gold in 6 weeks to confirm boosting phenomenon before offering any active management
options.rationale: QuantiFERON does not boost like the tuberculin skin test; repeat testing is not required to confirm a positive result. (Source: NTAC Position Statement on Latent TB Infection)
source_refs: NTAC Position Statement on Latent TB Infection

options.text: Offer treatment for latent tuberculosis infection with rifampicin 600 mg daily for 4 months with monthly liver enzyme monitoring
options.rationale: NTAC latent TB pathway offers a shorter, better-tolerated regimen (4 months rifampicin or 3 months rifampicin plus isoniazid) preferred over 9-month isoniazid for most adults, with monthly LFT monitoring. (Source: NTAC Position Statement on Latent TB Infection)
source_refs: NTAC Position Statement on Latent TB Infection

options.text: Refer for early morning sputum acid-fast bacilli smear x3 and TB PCR before any decision about latent tuberculosis treatment
options.rationale: Sputum testing is only indicated when active TB is suspected on symptoms or radiology; she is asymptomatic with a clear film and does not need sputum studies. (Source: NTAC Position Statement on Latent TB Infection)
source_refs: NTAC Position Statement on Latent TB Infection

explanation.summary: Latent tuberculosis infection is diagnosed by a positive interferon-gamma release assay (QuantiFERON-TB Gold or T-SPOT.TB) or a positive tuberculin skin test with a compatible risk profile, in the absence of clinical or radiological evidence of active disease. QuantiFERON does not cross-react with BCG or with most non-tuberculous mycobacteria. In Australia, NTAC offers treatment where the benefit outweighs the risk; healthcare workers, migrants from high-burden countries in the last 5 years, HIV, TNF-alpha inhibitor candidates and paediatric contacts are priority groups. Preferred regimens are 4 months of rifampicin (4R), 3 months of rifampicin plus isoniazid (3HR) or 3 months of once-weekly isoniazid plus rifapentine (3HP), all shorter and better tolerated than the traditional 9 months of isoniazid. Monthly clinical and LFT monitoring is standard. Baseline hepatitis B and C serology and pregnancy status are checked before starting.
key_points: QuantiFERON does not cross-react with BCG.
Latent TB treatment preferred: 4R, 3HR or 3HP over 9H.
Monthly clinical and LFT monitoring during treatment.
Sputum only if active TB suspected on symptoms or imaging.
explanation.pearls: For latent TB in a healthy adult, offer 4 months of rifampicin (4R) with monthly LFT monitoring; 9 months of isoniazid is now second choice due to hepatotoxicity and adherence.

sources.label: NTAC Position Statement on Latent TB Infection

stem:
A 68-year-old woman is brought to your emergency department by ambulance with 24 hours of urinary frequency, fever and worsening confusion. She has type 2 diabetes on metformin, hypertension on ramipril and chronic kidney disease stage 3 (baseline creatinine 140 micromol/L, eGFR 42 mL/min/1.73 m^2). She lives independently and is normally alert and oriented. She has no known drug allergies.

On arrival she is confused (GCS 13/15, disoriented to time and place), warm and vasodilated, and complaining of loin pain. Cardiovascular examination shows dual heart sounds without murmur. Chest is clear. Abdomen has right renal angle tenderness. Point-of-care venous lactate is 3.6 mmol/L (0.5-2.2). Urine dipstick shows blood 2+, leukocytes 3+ and nitrites positive. Her weight is 80 kg. She has no chills currently but had rigors overnight.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, blood pressure 88/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 96 percent on 4 L/min via nasal prong, temperature 39.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: GCS 13, warm vasodilated peripheries, right renal angle tenderness, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Venous lactate 3.6 mmol/L (0.5-2.2); urine dipstick blood 2+, leukocytes 3+, nitrites positive; creatinine 210 mcmol/L (from baseline 140)

lead_in: Within the first hour, which set of interventions best meets Australian sepsis pathway targets?

options.text: Blood cultures then intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g plus oral paracetamol and admit for further monitoring
options.rationale: Piperacillin-tazobactam is not first-line for community-acquired severe urosepsis in AU guidelines; ceftriaxone or amoxicillin plus gentamicin is preferred. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Sepsis in adults)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Sepsis in adults

options.text: Blood cultures then intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g and 500 mL normal saline infused over the next 4 hours as maintenance therapy alone
options.rationale: Fluid resuscitation for septic shock is 30 mL/kg crystalloid in the first hour, not 500 mL over 4 hours; this under-resuscitates. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Sepsis in adults)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Sepsis in adults

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g without blood cultures because she is already on empirical antibiotics and cultures will be unreliable
options.rationale: Blood cultures should be obtained before antibiotics whenever possible without delaying therapy; skipping them loses microbiological guidance. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Sepsis in adults)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Sepsis in adults

options.text: Serum lactate, blood cultures then intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g and 30 mL per kilogram intravenous crystalloid over the first hour
options.rationale: Every element listed is in the Hour-1 sepsis bundle for AU urosepsis; however this option omits repeat lactate to guide further resuscitation, which the AU bundle also requires within the first hour and this is delivered by option E.
source_refs: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Sepsis in adults

options.text: Blood cultures and lactate, then intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g and 30 mL per kilogram crystalloid, with repeat lactate at the end of the first hour
options.rationale: AU Sepsis Kills / Surviving Sepsis Hour-1 bundle: cultures, lactate, empirical antibiotic (ceftriaxone for community urosepsis) and 30 mL/kg crystalloid, with repeat lactate to guide further resuscitation. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Sepsis in adults)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Sepsis in adults

explanation.summary: The Australian Sepsis Kills and Surviving Sepsis campaign Hour-1 bundle applies to any adult with suspected sepsis and hypotension or lactate above 2 mmol/L. It comprises: measure serum lactate; obtain blood cultures (before antibiotics if possible without delay); administer broad-spectrum antibiotics within an hour; give 30 mL/kg intravenous crystalloid within 3 hours (aim for early completion) for hypotension or lactate at or above 4 mmol/L; and start vasopressors (usually noradrenaline) to keep mean arterial pressure at least 65 mmHg if fluids do not restore perfusion. Empirical antibiotic depends on source: ceftriaxone 2 g IV for community-acquired urosepsis or CAP, piperacillin-tazobactam plus vancomycin for hospital-acquired or neutropenic sepsis. Repeat lactate at the end of hour 1 guides fluid and vasopressor titration. Source control (e.g. drainage of an obstructed kidney) is arranged as soon as safely possible.
key_points: Hour-1 bundle: cultures, lactate, antibiotics, 30 mL/kg fluid, vasopressor if needed.
Ceftriaxone 2 g IV first-line for AU community-acquired urosepsis.
Give 30 mL/kg crystalloid within the first hour for hypotension or lactate over 4.
Repeat lactate to titrate resuscitation.
explanation.pearls: For adult community-acquired urosepsis, the Hour-1 bundle is lactate, cultures, IV ceftriaxone 2 g, 30 mL/kg crystalloid, then repeat lactate to guide vasopressor start.

sources.label: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Sepsis in adults
NSW Health SEPSIS KILLS Adult Pathway

stem:
A 46-year-old woman is brought to your emergency department by her husband with 2 days of vomiting, worsening fatigue and a 3-hour history of collapse. She has a background of primary autoimmune Addison's disease diagnosed 6 years ago, maintained on hydrocortisone 15 mg on waking and 5 mg at 2 pm plus fludrocortisone 100 micrograms daily, and has autoimmune hypothyroidism on thyroxine 100 micrograms daily. She was well until 3 days ago when she developed a gastroenteritis-like illness with vomiting; she was unable to keep her steroids down but did not increase her dose or seek care.

On arrival she is pale, cold, drowsy, and profoundly hypotensive. She has skin hyperpigmentation of the palmar creases and old buccal patches consistent with Addison's. She has no focal neurology. Point-of-care venous glucose is 2.6 mmol/L (3.5-6.0). Bedside biochemistry shows sodium 122 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 5.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), urea 12 mmol/L (2.5-7.5), creatinine 148 micromol/L (45-90) and eosinophils 0.6 x10^9/L (0.02-0.5).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128/min, blood pressure 74/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 35.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Pale, cold, drowsy, palmar and buccal hyperpigmentation, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 122 mmol/L (135-145); potassium 5.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.5); glucose 2.6 mmol/L (3.5-6.0); creatinine 148 mcmol/L (45-90); eosinophilia 0.6 x10^9/L (0.02-0.5)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg immediately followed by 1 litre 0.9 percent normal saline with 5 percent dextrose over the first hour
options.rationale: Addisonian crisis with hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia demands empirical IV hydrocortisone 100 mg without waiting for ACTH stimulation, plus saline with dextrose for volume and glucose. (Source: ESA Consensus Statement on Adrenal Insufficiency)
source_refs: ESA Consensus Statement on Adrenal Insufficiency

options.text: Intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg immediately with plans to perform a formal short synacthen test later this admission
options.rationale: Dexamethasone can be used if diagnosis is uncertain because it will not interfere with subsequent cortisol assay; however she has a confirmed diagnosis and hydrocortisone is preferred for its mineralocorticoid effect. (Source: ESA Consensus Statement on Adrenal Insufficiency)
source_refs: ESA Consensus Statement on Adrenal Insufficiency

options.text: Intravenous 3 percent hypertonic saline 100 mL bolus to correct her severe hyponatraemia before other measures are undertaken
options.rationale: Rapid sodium correction with hypertonic saline risks osmotic demyelination and does not address the underlying cortisol deficit. (Source: ESA Consensus Statement on Adrenal Insufficiency)
source_refs: ESA Consensus Statement on Adrenal Insufficiency

options.text: Intravenous 10 units short-acting insulin with 50 mL of 50 percent dextrose to correct hyperkalaemia as first-line therapy
options.rationale: Insulin-dextrose does not address the underlying cortisol deficit and risks worsening her existing hypoglycaemia; the hyperkalaemia typically corrects with hydrocortisone and saline. (Source: ESA Consensus Statement on Adrenal Insufficiency)
source_refs: ESA Consensus Statement on Adrenal Insufficiency

options.text: Oral hydrocortisone 60 mg stat with intravenous 0.9 percent normal saline 500 mL over 30 minutes and paediatric admission
options.rationale: Oral therapy is inappropriate in the vomiting shocked patient and cannot be relied upon; IV hydrocortisone is required. (Source: ESA Consensus Statement on Adrenal Insufficiency)
source_refs: ESA Consensus Statement on Adrenal Insufficiency

explanation.summary: Addisonian (adrenal) crisis presents as hypotension, hypovolaemia, altered consciousness, gastrointestinal symptoms, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia in a patient with primary adrenal insufficiency. Typical triggers are intercurrent illness with vomiting, missed steroid doses, or a stressor without stress-dose adjustment. Empirical IV hydrocortisone 100 mg immediately (then 50 mg every 6 hours or a 200 mg per 24-hour infusion) is the priority, with 1 litre 0.9 percent normal saline (with 5 percent dextrose if hypoglycaemic) in the first hour and further crystalloid guided by response. Hyperkalaemia and hyponatraemia typically correct with steroid and fluid; specific therapy for either is rarely needed. Once oral tolerance returns, transition to double-dose oral hydrocortisone tapering over a few days back to baseline. Sick-day education (double-dose oral for illness; parenteral hydrocortisone kit at home) prevents recurrence.
key_points: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg immediately; do not wait for ACTH stimulation.
1 litre normal saline (with dextrose if hypoglycaemic) in the first hour.
Sodium and potassium usually correct with steroid and fluid alone.
Sick-day plan and home parenteral kit prevent recurrence.
explanation.pearls: For a known Addisonian in shock with hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia, give IV hydrocortisone 100 mg and 1 litre normal saline with 5 percent dextrose in the first hour.

sources.label: ESA Consensus Statement on Adrenal Insufficiency

stem:
A 58-year-old man is brought to your regional emergency department with 45 minutes of sudden severe tearing chest pain radiating to his back. He has poorly controlled hypertension (usual blood pressures around 165/95 mmHg), a 30-pack-year smoking history and takes amlodipine 5 mg daily. He denies drug allergies.

On arrival he is pale and diaphoretic. Cardiovascular examination shows a soft early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge and a blood pressure differential of 40 mmHg between arms (right 210/104 mmHg, left 170/98 mmHg). Peripheral pulses are all palpable but the left radial is weak. His neurology is intact and there is no focal weakness. Point-of-care troponin is elevated at 62 ng/L (<14). ECG shows sinus tachycardia at 118/min without acute ST changes. Chest radiograph shows a widened mediastinum. Bedside transthoracic echocardiography suggests an intimal flap in the ascending aorta and a small pericardial effusion. Cardiothoracic retrieval to the tertiary centre has been called and estimated at 45 minutes.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, blood pressure right arm 210/104 mmHg, left arm 170/98 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 98 percent on 4 L/min via nasal prong, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Pale, diaphoretic, soft early diastolic murmur, 40 mmHg inter-arm BP differential, weak left radial pulse, neurology intact
data_table.Investigations: Troponin 62 ng/L (<14); ECG sinus tachycardia; CXR widened mediastinum; TTE intimal flap in ascending aorta with small pericardial effusion

lead_in: While awaiting retrieval, what is the single most appropriate initial pharmacological plan?

options.text: Intravenous nitroglycerin infusion titrated to a systolic blood pressure of 120 mmHg without any prior heart rate control agent
options.rationale: Vasodilator without prior beta blockade causes reflex tachycardia that increases aortic shear stress and worsens the dissection; heart rate control precedes blood pressure reduction. (Source: RACP Aortic Dissection Consensus)
source_refs: RACP Aortic Dissection Consensus

options.text: Intravenous esmolol infusion titrated to heart rate 60 to 80/min, then intravenous glyceryl trinitrate to systolic blood pressure 100 to 120 mmHg
options.rationale: AU management of Type A dissection: heart rate control with beta blockade first (esmolol or labetalol) then vasodilator to achieve systolic BP 100 to 120 mmHg, reducing aortic shear stress before surgery. (Source: RACP Aortic Dissection Consensus)
source_refs: RACP Aortic Dissection Consensus

options.text: Intravenous aspirin 300 mg plus intravenous heparin loading dose of 5000 units for suspected acute coronary syndrome
options.rationale: Anticoagulation and antiplatelet therapy are contraindicated in acute aortic dissection because they worsen bleeding into the false lumen and pericardium. (Source: RACP Aortic Dissection Consensus)
source_refs: RACP Aortic Dissection Consensus

options.text: Intravenous hydralazine 20 mg bolus every 30 minutes titrated to systolic blood pressure below 120 mmHg without any beta blocker
options.rationale: Hydralazine causes reflex tachycardia and increases aortic shear stress; a beta blocker must be used first for rate control. (Source: RACP Aortic Dissection Consensus)
source_refs: RACP Aortic Dissection Consensus

options.text: Intravenous morphine 5 mg boluses titrated to pain control while awaiting retrieval, with no antihypertensive or heart rate agent
options.rationale: Analgesia is important but does not address the ongoing aortic shear stress driving dissection propagation; rate and BP control are the immediate priorities. (Source: RACP Aortic Dissection Consensus)
source_refs: RACP Aortic Dissection Consensus

explanation.summary: Acute aortic dissection is classified by the Stanford system as Type A (involving the ascending aorta) or Type B (distal to the left subclavian). Type A is a surgical emergency requiring urgent cardiothoracic repair; Type B is usually medically managed unless complicated by malperfusion, rupture or refractory pain. Medical management focuses on reducing aortic wall shear stress: heart rate is targeted first with intravenous beta blockade (esmolol or labetalol) to 60 to 80/min, then blood pressure with a vasodilator (glyceryl trinitrate or sodium nitroprusside) to a systolic 100 to 120 mmHg. Vasodilators without prior beta blockade cause reflex tachycardia and increase shear stress. Anticoagulation and antiplatelet therapy are contraindicated. Analgesia with intravenous opioid is important. Retrieval to a cardiothoracic centre is prioritised for Type A dissection.
key_points: Heart rate control with beta blocker before vasodilator in dissection.
Target heart rate 60 to 80/min, systolic BP 100 to 120 mmHg.
Anticoagulation and antiplatelet therapy are contraindicated.
Type A dissection is a surgical emergency requiring urgent repair.
explanation.pearls: For acute Type A aortic dissection, start IV esmolol to target heart rate 60 to 80/min, then IV glyceryl trinitrate to systolic 100 to 120 mmHg; never vasodilate before rate control.

stem:
A 62-year-old woman presents to your emergency department with 4 hours of headache and blurred vision. She was diagnosed with essential hypertension 5 years ago and takes irbesartan 300 mg and amlodipine 10 mg daily, but has been non-adherent for 6 weeks due to a prescription lapse. She has no history of stroke or heart failure and does not smoke.

On arrival she is drowsy but rousable, oriented to person only. Fundoscopy shows bilateral flame haemorrhages and cotton wool spots without papilloedema. Cardiovascular examination shows an S4 gallop without S3, no pulmonary crackles and no peripheral oedema. Neurological examination shows no lateralising signs and reflexes are symmetric. Urinalysis has 2+ protein and blood. Bedside creatinine is 148 micromol/L (from baseline 84 micromol/L on record 3 months ago). Non-contrast computed tomography of the head shows no intracranial haemorrhage. ECG shows sinus rhythm with left ventricular hypertrophy criteria and no acute ischaemia.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, blood pressure 232/142 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, oriented to person only, no focal neurology, bilateral flame haemorrhages and cotton wool spots without papilloedema, S4 gallop
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 148 mcmol/L (baseline 84 3 months ago); urinalysis 2+ protein, 2+ blood; ECG LVH criteria; CT head no haemorrhage

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial pharmacological plan?

options.text: Oral captopril 25 mg with observation over 2 hours before considering further dose escalation or parenteral antihypertensive agents
options.rationale: Oral therapy is too slow and unreliable in a hypertensive emergency with end-organ damage; IV therapy titratable in a monitored setting is required. (Source: Australian eTG: Cardiovascular - Hypertensive emergency)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Cardiovascular - Hypertensive emergency

options.text: Intravenous nifedipine short-acting 10 mg sublingual bolus for rapid blood pressure reduction to a target of 140/90 mmHg within 30 minutes
options.rationale: Sublingual short-acting nifedipine causes precipitous uncontrolled drops in BP and risks stroke; it is not recommended for hypertensive emergency. (Source: Australian eTG: Cardiovascular - Hypertensive emergency)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Cardiovascular - Hypertensive emergency

options.text: Intravenous labetalol 20 mg bolus repeated every 10 minutes as needed to reduce mean arterial pressure by no more than 25 percent in the first hour
options.rationale: AU hypertensive emergency management is IV labetalol (or glyceryl trinitrate) with staged reduction of MAP by no more than 25 percent in the first hour to prevent watershed injury. (Source: Australian eTG: Cardiovascular - Hypertensive emergency)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Cardiovascular - Hypertensive emergency

options.text: Restart irbesartan 300 mg and amlodipine 10 mg orally and observe on the ward for 48 hours before further consideration
options.rationale: Oral therapy is inadequate for hypertensive emergency with encephalopathy; parenteral titratable therapy is required and simply restarting missed medications is unsafe. (Source: Australian eTG: Cardiovascular - Hypertensive emergency)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Cardiovascular - Hypertensive emergency

options.text: Intravenous glyceryl trinitrate 5 microgram per minute titrated as sole agent to systolic below 120 mmHg within the first 30 minutes
options.rationale: Reducing systolic below 120 mmHg in the first 30 minutes exceeds AU targets and risks cerebral watershed injury; MAP should fall by no more than 25 percent in the first hour. (Source: Australian eTG: Cardiovascular - Hypertensive emergency)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Cardiovascular - Hypertensive emergency

explanation.summary: Hypertensive emergency is severe hypertension (usually diastolic above 120 mmHg or systolic above 180 mmHg) with acute end-organ damage: encephalopathy, papilloedema, acute kidney injury, pulmonary oedema, myocardial ischaemia or acute aortic syndrome. Treatment is parenteral titratable therapy in a monitored setting, with a staged reduction: mean arterial pressure by no more than 25 percent in the first hour, then to 160/100 mmHg over the next 2 to 6 hours, and to near baseline over 24 to 48 hours. Faster reduction risks cerebral, renal or coronary watershed injury. Choice of agent depends on the target organ: labetalol or nicardipine for encephalopathy or renal failure; glyceryl trinitrate for pulmonary oedema or acute coronary syndrome; hydralazine and labetalol for pre-eclampsia. Sublingual nifedipine is unsafe due to uncontrolled precipitous drops. Investigate for a secondary cause once BP is controlled.
key_points: Emergency = severe hypertension plus acute end-organ damage.
Reduce MAP by no more than 25 percent in the first hour.
Labetalol or nicardipine for encephalopathy; nitrate for pulmonary oedema.
Sublingual short-acting nifedipine is unsafe.
explanation.pearls: In hypertensive emergency with encephalopathy, use IV labetalol 20 to 80 mg boluses to reduce mean arterial pressure by no more than 25 percent in the first hour.

stem:
A 44-year-old woman presents to your endocrinology clinic with 8 months of weight gain (12 kg), facial rounding, easy bruising, three vertebral compression fractures on recent spinal imaging and new hypertension diagnosed 4 months ago. She has type 2 diabetes for which metformin was added 2 months ago. She has no other medications. She works night shifts as a security officer and reports irregular sleep for 3 years.

On examination she has central obesity, thin bruised skin over the shins and upper limbs, and purple striae over the abdomen more than 1 cm wide. Blood pressure is 168/98 mmHg. Her random cortisol at 3 pm is 620 nmol/L (100-540). Overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test: morning cortisol 210 nmol/L (target below 50). A 24-hour urinary free cortisol is 850 nmol/day (55-330). Late night salivary cortisol collected on 2 different days: 22 and 18 nmol/L (below 3 in typical circadian rhythm). Her plasma ACTH is 62 ng/L (10-60). Thyroid function, prolactin, and IGF-1 are within normal limits. She has no visual field defect.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82/min, blood pressure 168/98 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Central obesity, thin bruised skin, purple abdominal striae >1 cm wide, blood pressure 168/98 mmHg, no visual field defect
data_table.Investigations: 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression cortisol 210 nmol/L (target <50); 24-hour urinary free cortisol 850 nmol/day (55-330); late night salivary cortisol 22 and 18 nmol/L; plasma ACTH 62 ng/L (10-60)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat the 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test in 6 months given her night-shift lifestyle likely accounts for the abnormal circadian result
options.rationale: Three separate first-line tests are positive with clinical features and morbidity; delay for repeat testing is unsafe and the shift-work confounder does not explain all three abnormal tests. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing's Syndrome Guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Cushing's Syndrome Guideline

options.text: Non-contrast computed tomography of both adrenals to look for a unilateral adrenal adenoma before further biochemical testing
options.rationale: Her ACTH is in the mid-normal range, suggesting ACTH-dependent Cushing's rather than an adrenal source; imaging the adrenals first would miss the driver. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing's Syndrome Guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Cushing's Syndrome Guideline

options.text: Serum aldosterone to renin ratio to screen for primary hyperaldosteronism as the explanation of her hypertension and hypokalaemia
options.rationale: Her hypertension and osteoporotic fractures are explained by Cushing's, which she meets diagnostic criteria for; primary aldosteronism does not explain the striae, cortisol excess or dexamethasone non-suppression. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing's Syndrome Guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Cushing's Syndrome Guideline

options.text: High-dose 8 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test followed by pituitary magnetic resonance imaging if suppression occurs
options.rationale: Cushing's is biochemically confirmed and ACTH-dependent; the high-dose DST (with or without pituitary MRI and inferior petrosal sinus sampling) discriminates pituitary from ectopic ACTH sources per Endocrine Society guidance. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing's Syndrome Guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Cushing's Syndrome Guideline

options.text: Empirical trial of metyrapone 250 mg 3 times daily to reduce cortisol synthesis before further diagnostic imaging is requested
options.rationale: Medical adrenolysis is a temporising measure before surgery, not a diagnostic step; localisation of the ACTH source is required. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing's Syndrome Guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Cushing's Syndrome Guideline

explanation.summary: Diagnosis of Cushing's syndrome follows a two-step approach: confirm autonomous cortisol excess, then identify the source. First-line screening tests are 24-hour urinary free cortisol on 2 separate collections, late-night salivary cortisol on 2 different nights, and 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test; two abnormal tests confirm the diagnosis. Once confirmed, plasma ACTH divides into ACTH-independent (ACTH suppressed, source is adrenal) and ACTH-dependent (ACTH detectable or elevated, source is pituitary or ectopic). For ACTH-dependent Cushing's, a high-dose 8 mg overnight DST with pituitary MRI is next; suppression at high dose plus a pituitary lesion supports Cushing's disease. Non-suppression, no visible pituitary lesion, or discordance prompts inferior petrosal sinus sampling. Ectopic ACTH sources (bronchial carcinoid, small cell lung cancer, medullary thyroid cancer, phaeochromocytoma) usually do not suppress at high dose. Confounders for the low-dose DST include night-shift work, oestrogens, and CYP450-inducing drugs.
key_points: Two abnormal first-line tests confirm Cushing's biochemically.
ACTH divides into independent (adrenal) and dependent (pituitary or ectopic).
High-dose DST plus pituitary MRI localise ACTH-dependent Cushing's.
Ectopic ACTH usually does not suppress at high dose.
explanation.pearls: After confirming Cushing's biochemically with two positive first-line tests and a non-suppressed ACTH, proceed to a high-dose 8 mg dexamethasone suppression test with pituitary MRI to distinguish pituitary from ectopic source.

stem:
A 54-year-old man presents to your emergency department with 4 days of progressive limb weakness, initially in the arms, now involving his legs. He noted double vision on waking today and difficulty swallowing sips of water. He had a diarrhoeal illness 2 weeks ago that resolved without treatment. He has no other medical history and takes no medications.

On examination he is alert with bilateral partial ophthalmoplegia and a downbeating nystagmus on lateral gaze. Cranial nerves show weakness of eye abduction bilaterally and mild bulbar dysfunction with pooling of secretions. Limb tone is reduced, power 3/5 proximally and 4/5 distally in all limbs. Deep tendon reflexes are absent throughout. Sensation is normal to pinprick and vibration. Coordination testing shows marked truncal ataxia with inability to sit unsupported. Forced vital capacity at the bedside is 1.4 L (predicted 4.2 L). Lumbar puncture shows CSF protein 1.6 g/L (0.15-0.45), glucose 3.8 mmol/L (2.2-3.9), and 2 lymphocytes/microL (0-5). MRI brain and cervical spine are normal.

data_table.Examination: Alert, bilateral partial ophthalmoplegia, downbeating nystagmus, truncal ataxia, generalised areflexia, symmetric limb weakness with intact sensation
data_table.Investigations: CSF protein 1.6 g/L (0.15-0.45), 2 lymphocytes/mcL (0-5); MRI brain and cervical spine normal; forced vital capacity 1.4 L (predicted 4.2 L)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 5 days as first-line therapy for suspected multiple sclerosis relapse presenting acutely
options.rationale: Steroids do not help Guillain-Barre or its variants and are potentially harmful; the CSF albuminocytological dissociation and reflex loss with recent Campylobacter-like illness point to Miller Fisher-Guillain-Barre overlap. (Source: Australian eTG: Neurology - Guillain-Barre)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Neurology - Guillain-Barre

options.text: Intravenous edrophonium 10 mg to establish the diagnosis of myasthenic crisis by symptomatic improvement of ptosis and swallowing
options.rationale: Areflexia and CSF albuminocytological dissociation are not features of myasthenia; edrophonium (Tensilon) is not appropriate here. (Source: Australian eTG: Neurology - Guillain-Barre)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Neurology - Guillain-Barre

options.text: Intravenous acyclovir 10 mg per kilogram every 8 hours empirically for herpes simplex brainstem encephalitis while awaiting further imaging
options.rationale: MRI brainstem is normal and CSF pleocytosis is absent; HSV encephalitis does not fit and IV acyclovir does not treat Guillain-Barre or Miller Fisher. (Source: Australian eTG: Neurology - Guillain-Barre)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Neurology - Guillain-Barre

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g plus dexamethasone 10 mg for suspected brainstem meningoencephalitis pending microbiology results
options.rationale: CSF shows albuminocytological dissociation without pleocytosis; bacterial meningitis is unlikely and neither antibiotic nor steroid treats Miller Fisher. (Source: Australian eTG: Neurology - Guillain-Barre)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Neurology - Guillain-Barre

options.text: Intravenous immunoglobulin 0.4 g per kilogram daily for 5 days, admit to a high-dependency unit and monitor forced vital capacity 4-hourly
options.rationale: The clinical picture (ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia with limb weakness) plus CSF albuminocytological dissociation is Miller Fisher-Guillain-Barre overlap; IVIG 0.4 g/kg daily for 5 days plus respiratory monitoring is standard AU therapy. (Source: Australian eTG: Neurology - Guillain-Barre)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Neurology - Guillain-Barre

explanation.summary: Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS) is an acute inflammatory polyneuropathy typically preceded by Campylobacter, CMV, EBV or Mycoplasma infection, with ascending symmetric weakness, areflexia, autonomic dysfunction and eventual respiratory involvement. Miller Fisher syndrome (MFS) is a variant defined by ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and areflexia (anti-GQ1b antibody positive in over 90 percent), and overlap syndromes are common. Diagnosis relies on the clinical picture plus CSF albuminocytological dissociation (raised protein, normal cell count, may be normal in the first week) and demyelinating pattern on nerve conduction studies. Treatment is IVIG 0.4 g/kg daily for 5 days or plasma exchange (5 sessions over 2 weeks) - the two are equally effective, and steroids do not help. Respiratory monitoring with 4-hourly FVC is critical: FVC below 20 mL/kg, negative inspiratory force below -30 cmH2O or bulbar dysfunction prompts HDU/ICU admission and consideration of intubation.
key_points: Miller Fisher triad: ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia (anti-GQ1b positive).
CSF albuminocytological dissociation supports GBS spectrum.
IVIG or plasma exchange are equally effective; steroids do not help.
Monitor FVC 4-hourly; intubate for FVC below 20 mL/kg or bulbar failure.
explanation.pearls: For Miller Fisher-Guillain-Barre overlap, give IVIG 0.4 g/kg daily for 5 days and monitor FVC 4-hourly; intubate for FVC below 20 mL/kg or bulbar failure.
